segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On that day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Large crowds gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat down, while the whole crowd stood on the shore.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he told them many things in parables, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Look! A sower went out to sow.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and ate them up.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Others fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and they sprang up immediately because the soil had no depth,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but when the sun rose they were scorched, and because they had no root they withered.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Others fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Others fell on the good soil and produced a crop—some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let the one who has ears hear.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then the disciples came and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why do you speak to them in parables?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Because to you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of the heavens, but to them it has not been given.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For whoever has will be given more and will have an abundance; but whoever does not have, even what they have will be taken away from them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: This is why I speak to them in parables: because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In them the prophecy of Isaiah is being fulfilled, which says: ‘You will hear and hear but never understand; you will look and look but never see.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they have barely heard, and they have shut their eyes; otherwise they might see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I would heal them.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For truly I tell you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: You, then, hear the parable of the sower.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in that person’s heart. This is the one sown along the path.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for the one sown on the rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but has no root within and lasts only a short time; when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, such a person immediately falls away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for the one sown among the thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the worry of this age and the deceitfulness of wealth choke the word, and it becomes unfruitful.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for the one sown on the good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it, who indeed bears fruit and yields—one a hundredfold, another sixty, another thirty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He set another parable before them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of the heavens may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But while people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When the plants sprouted and produced a crop, then the weeds appeared as well.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The householder’s slaves came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? Where then did the weeds come from?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ The slaves said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and collect them?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But he said, ‘No, for in collecting the weeds you might uproot the wheat along with them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Collect the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He set another parable before them, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of the heavens is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the sky come and nest in its branches.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He told them another parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of the heavens is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and he said nothing to them without a parable,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that what was spoken through the prophet might be fulfilled:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The field is the world, and the good seed—these are the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So just as the weeds are collected and burned with fire, so it will be at the end of the age.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will collect out of his kingdom everything that causes stumbling and those who practice lawlessness,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and they will throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Let the one who has ears hear.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The kingdom of the heavens is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and hid; and in his joy he goes and sells everything he has and buys that field.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a merchant searching for fine pearls.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When he found one pearl of great value, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Again, the kingdom of the heavens is like a dragnet that was cast into the sea and gathered fish of every kind.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: When it was full, they hauled it up onto the shore, sat down, and collected the good ones into containers, but threw the bad ones out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will go out and separate the evil from among the righteous

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and throw them into the furnace of fire. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Have you understood all these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Therefore every scribe who has been made a disciple for the kingdom of the heavens is like a householder who brings out of his storeroom things new and old.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus had finished these parables, he moved on from there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Coming to his hometown, he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Where did this man get this wisdom and these deeds of power?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: Is this not the carpenter’s son? Is his mother not called Mary, and his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: And are not all his sisters here with us? Where then did this man get all these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he did not do many deeds of power there, because of their unbelief.

notes.note: Most English versions have “mysteries.” In Jewish Greek of the period this was the ordinary word for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose, whereas English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding. Lexicons give “secret” as a primary gloss, and several mainstream versions use it in this saying, though many scholars defend “mystery” as an established technical term.

Matthew’s Greek is plural here, as it is every time he uses this phrase, reflecting a Semitic way of speaking about God’s dwelling. Most translations flatten it to “heaven”; the plural is kept because a first-century hearer would have noticed it. The meaning is the same as “kingdom of God” in the other Gospels.

The traditional rendering is “tribulation,” which many readers now hear as the name of a specific end-time period. The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on someone. Lexicons agree on the sense, and English versions vary among “tribulation,” “affliction,” “trouble” and “distress.”

The King James Version has “is offended,” which now suggests hurt feelings. The verb means to be tripped up so as to abandon one’s loyalty, and most modern versions also render it “falls away” here. The same verb appears in verse 57, where the sense is that people were affronted by Jesus, and it is translated “took offense” there.

Many versions have “the cares of the world” or “the worries of this life.” The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, and it reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. It is the same word used in “the end of the age” in verses 39, 40 and 49, and a different word from the one translated “world” in verse 38.

The Greek word names a particular weed, generally identified as darnel, a grass that looks very much like wheat until the ears form. That is why the weeds only become apparent when the crop appears (verse 26), and why pulling them early risks uprooting the wheat. Older versions call them “tares.”

Most English versions have “servants.” The Greek word ordinarily meant a slave, a person owned by the householder, and a first-century reader would have understood it so. “Servant” suggests a hired employee, which is a different Greek word.

The measure named here was a dry measure usually estimated at around thirteen liters, so three of them is a very large batch of flour—enough bread to feed well over a hundred people. The exact size is uncertain, but the point of the picture is that a small amount of leaven works through a huge quantity of dough.

notes.traditional: from the foundation of the world
notes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 78:2. Many manuscripts read “from the foundation of the world”; the Greek text translated here has the shorter reading without “of the world,” though the meaning is the same. A few manuscripts also read “through the prophet Isaiah,” which is probably a copyist’s slip, since the words are not from Isaiah.

The King James Version has “all things that offend”; modern versions have “all causes of sin” or “everything that causes sin.” The Greek word means a trap or obstacle that makes someone fall, and figuratively whatever leads a person into sin or ruin. Here the collective may include people as well as things.

notes.phrase: made a disciple for the kingdom of the heavens
notes.traditional: instructed unto the kingdom of heaven
notes.note: The Greek verb can mean either “become a disciple” or “be instructed,” and the kingdom may be that for which, or about which, the scribe is trained. Versions accordingly vary between “trained for the kingdom,” “instructed about the kingdom” and “become a disciple of the kingdom.” The rendering here keeps the link with the word “disciple,” which the Greek makes audible.

Traditional renderings are “mighty works” or “miracles.” The Greek is simply the ordinary word for power, used in the plural for acts that display it, and “deeds of power” keeps that connection visible. There is no dispute about the meaning, and “miracles” is an equally acceptable translation.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and versions split between “servant,” “slave” and “bondservant,” so readers would be misled if it varied by chapter.
Recurs in the Gospels and Paul, and translators divide between “leaven” and “yeast”; the cross-references (Matthew 16, 1 Corinthians 5, Galatians 5) depend on one consistent word.
Recurs in Matthew, Paul, Hebrews and 1 John, and is rendered variously as “lawlessness,” “iniquity,” “evil” or “wickedness.”

candidates.rendering: the evil one (substantive, personal); evil (of people)
candidates.reason: The substantive with the article is ambiguous between “the evil one” and “evil” in several key passages (Matthew 5:37; 6:13; John 17:15), and the adjective varies between “evil” and “wicked,” so a single policy is needed.
Used of the Lake of Galilee across the Gospels, where some versions say “lake” and others “sea”; the choice should be uniform.

warnings: Verse 57: σκανδαλίζω is not rendered with a register form (cause to stumble; stumble / be made to stumble; fall away; take offense / give offense; be made to fall) and has no register-exception note.
